catalog_quote: [p.9, sec. 1.3 Tone] Kumam is a tone language, exhibiting a low tone, a high tone, a falling tone, a rising tone, a downstep high tone and a double downstep high tone, which contrast on a phonetic level. However, a low toneme and a high toneme are posited in underlying representations. There are a few tone sandhi rules which have the effect of altering the underlying tonal representation of a word in particular environments. [p.6, sec. 1.2.2] The vowel sandhi rules are applied to unstressed vowels only. When a word ending in a vowel is followed by a word beginning with a vowel, if the vowels are stressed, vowel coalescence does not take place between them. For instance, when the preposition ɪ 'at, in, to' is followed by the noun ɔt 'house', the vowel of the preposition is not deleted because both the vowel of the preposition ɪ 'at, in, to' and that of the noun ɔt 'house' are stressed. [p.57, sec. 1.4.2.3] However, vowel sandhi occurs only in unstressed vowels. All lexical tonemes are preserved though vowels are deleted according to vowel sandhi rules. The final vowel of the noun jame 'things' may be deleted because it is not stressed, while the vowel of the noun le 'animal' is not deleted because it is stressed. ... When possessors begin with a vowel, the possessive particle can be deleted before the following vowels, because the possessive particle is not stressed.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kumam is analysed as a tone language (underlying L and H tonemes; surface L, H, falling, rising, downstep H, double-downstep H). The grammar has no section on stress and never states where word stress falls; 'stress' is invoked only as a blocking condition on vowel sandhi: monosyllabic content words and the preposition ɪ are 'stressed', while grammatical particles (possessive a, attributive a) and the final vowel of disyllabic jamé 'things' are 'not stressed' (which would be consistent with non-final/stem stress, but the author does not say so).
new_statements.exceptions: None; only that pronominal object suffixes and topic boundaries block vowel sandhi independently of stress (p.6-7).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is lexical and grammatical (aspect marked by suprasegmental L morpheme); tone sandhi operates across 'phonological units' (≈ words). The stress remarks concern word-level stress of vowels at word edges in connected speech; p.379 adds that Kumam, as a tone language, does 'not make use of stress to express information structure in most cases'.
new_statements.identity_note: All three Hieda works describe the same variety: Kumam as spoken in Kaberamaido/Soroti/Serere districts, central Uganda (one principal consultant, fieldwork 1999-2012); no dialect differentiation is made. Glottocode kuma1275, ISO kdi.

new_statements.quote: [p.6] The vowel sandhi rule is applied to unstressed vowels only. When a word ending in a vowel is followed by a word beginning with a vowel, vowel coalescence does not take place if either the vowel of the preceding word or that of the following word is stressed. For instance, when the preposition í 'at, in, to' is followed by the noun ót 'house', the vowel of the preposition is not deleted because both the vowel of the preposition and that of the noun are stressed (9). [p.70] However, vowel sandhi occurs only in unstressed vowels. All lexical tonemes are preserved though vowels are deleted according to vowel sandhi rules. The vowel of the noun jame 'things' in final position is deleted, because the vowel is not stressed (15). The vowel of the noun le 'animal' is not deleted because it is stressed (16).

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing statement from Hieda 2013 (tone language, H/L tonemes, no word-stress statement) and with our earlier reading finding; the sandhi 'stressed/unstressed' wording on p.6 is verbatim the same as Hieda 2013 p.6 and Hieda 2010 fn.5. Refines only in adding the p.70/p.74 sandhi passages and the p.35 Swahili-loan remark; the catalog record itself has an empty rule, and this work supplies nothing to fill it with a stress placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The work has no section on stress and never states where word stress falls. Kumam is described as a tone language: four phonetic level tones (L, H, downstep H, double downstep H) plus falling and rising, reduced to two underlying tonemes H and L (sec. 3.1-3.2, pp.9-11); every noun carries a lexical tonal pattern (14 tone classes, sec. 3.9, pp.31-36) and the dictionary entries are marked for tone class, not for stress (vocabulary pp.92, 356 conventions pages). The only mention of stress is 'stressed/unstressed vowel' as a condition on vowel-sandhi (coalescence/deletion): monosyllabic preposition í and nouns ót 'house', lé 'animal' count as stressed; the final vowel of jamé 'things', the possessive particle a and the attributive particle a(H) count as unstressed (pp.6, 70, 74). No rule for placing stress is given. The one use of 'accent' as prominence is about Swahili, not Kumam: tone class XII loanwords' H + downstep-H ending 'correspond to the accent pattern of the Swahili language, whose words always have a pitch accent on the second syllable from right end' (p.35).
new_statements.exceptions: none stated for stress; the 'stressed' vs 'not stressed' labels apply to specific morphemes (monosyllabic content words vs final vowel of jamé and the particles a / a(H)) as a sandhi condition only.
new_statements.identity_note: Hieda's data are from one consultant, fieldwork 1999-2009; Kumam of the Kaberamaido, Soroti, Serere and Kyoga districts of central Uganda (Grammatical Notes p.1). No dialect is singled out.
